issue_body: It seems to be a less efficient way to iterate over a file rather than just iterating over it directly. It's only yielding 8 kB chunks at a time. The intention of `wsgi.file_wrapper` in WSGI is to expose more efficient file sending from the operating system. The key is optional, our `wrap_file` function is allowed to return the file unchanged if it's not set.

comments.author: davidism
comments.body:
`FileWrapper` should still be kept internally and used as the default for `wrap_file`. Still deprecate from the public API.

`FileWrapper` is still useful because otherwise `iter(file)` is line-based, which is completely arbitrary for binary files. Noticed that Python 3.14 updated `io.DEFAULT_BUFFER_SIZE` to 128 KiB, but `wrap_file` defaults to 8 KiB. Some quick socket tests shows about a 3x improvement by increasing the default size to 128 KiB. Gunicorn and Waitress provide file wrappers with lower defaults, so this will improve them as well.

issue_title: Move header and body checks to sans-IO `Response`
issue_body:
Similar to `apply_conditions` and `apply_range`, add a `_prepare_response` method to remove headers and body based on request method or response status code. That's currently handled during `get_wsgi_headers` and `get_app_iter`, which is specific to WSGI. But it doesn't do any IO (it clears the body, but that's not a read or write to the stream), so it could be a method on the sans-IO base `Response`.

It seems like most WSGI and ASGI servers handle this, but given that it's not part of the spec we can't safely assume that all do, some might assume the app does it. Also, `Response.from_app` and some other utilities can run another WSGI app internally, so it's probably better to produce a "valid" response in that case.

The method would be private, to be called by the response class at the start of `get_wsgi_response` and whatever the ASGI equivalent would be.

comments.author: davidism
comments.body: `Response.set_data` is a sync method in Quart as well. So it can be part of the sans-IO class, with a concrete implementation in the subclasses.

comments.author: davidism
comments.body: `set_data` won't help here, since it also has behavior that sets the content length. For example, I'd expect `set_data(None)` to clear the content length. That's not useful for `prepare_response`, a `HEAD` request requires an empty body but the correct content length for `GET`. We'd probably want a `_clear_body` method for our internal use.

comments.author: davidism
comments.body:
After investigating the behavior around `Response.freeze`, I'm convinced that it can't guarantee a reusable response. Because of that, `get_wsgi_response` doesn't need to avoid modifying the response in place (with the new `prepare_response` method).

- They can have `call_on_close` callbacks that would not be valid in a subsequent request context. In fact, until https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/pull/3325 the original body's `close` method would have been kept around for every subsequent reuse. `freeze` could call `close`, but that wouldn't solve the other problems.
- They can be a streaming response, where buffering the generator would defeat the purpose.
- The can be a file response, where buffering the file would be redundant (it's already "cached" in the filesystem) and would prevent any `wsgi.file_wrapper` optimizations from the server.
- `make_conditional` (split into `apply_conditions` and `apply_range` in Werkzeug 3.2) modifies the response in-place (the status or raising an `HTTPException`) based on the current request's precondition and range headers. This is dependent on the current time and data (such as file modified time and contents).
- `get_wsgi_response` on the other hand does not modify the response in place, but any of those in place modifications it's avoiding are already dependent on the response having a specific status. Therefore, caching the response with that status would mean the same headers are sent every single time anyway. There's no point in avoiding the in-place modification.
- Support for reusing responses was added in 2010 https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/commit/430ded16cf3a4145139df51c46f8e6c56470ba6f, seemingly with the goal of caching, but didn't seem to consider any of the above.

@sh4nks @john0isaac This is something to consider for Flask-Caching. I think the docs need to be much clearer that response objects in general cannot be safely cached and reused. That doesn't mean there's a lot of views where none of the above applies and it is safe, but the docs should probably push more towards caching smaller parts of the processing, rather than the response itself.

Yeah we have had an issue before about unpicklable objects and I suggested they use freeze but I also suggested that they can write their own serializer to parse and maybe filter what to pickle which will eliminate any issues you face with freeze.

issue_title: dev server doesn't close response iterable when client resets connection
issue_body:
If the client resets the connection while the dev server is sending a response, the response iterable's `close()` is never called. With `send_file` this leaves the file open, and you get `ResourceWarning: unclosed file` later. Under `pytest -W error` that fails an unrelated test. I see it in browser tests when a page closes while an asset is still downloading.

```python
import socket
import struct
import threading
import time

from werkzeug.serving import make_server


class Body:
    def __iter__(self):
        for _ in range(1000):
            yield b"x" * 65536

    def close(self):
        print("closed")


def app(environ, start_response):
    start_response("200 OK", [("Content-Type", "text/plain")])
    return Body()


server = make_server("127.0.0.1", 0, app)
threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

sock = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", server.port))
sock.sendall(b"GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: localhost\r\n\r\n")
sock.recv(4096)
# close with RST instead of FIN
sock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_LINGER, struct.pack("ii", 1, 0))
sock.close()
time.sleep(1)
server.shutdown()
```

Expected: `closed` is printed.

Actual: nothing is printed (10 of 10 runs).

Cause: `write()` fails with the reset, then the `finally` block in `run_wsgi` drains the socket before closing the iterable. The socket is readable because of the reset, so `self.rfile.read(10_000_000)` raises `ConnectionResetError`, which skips `selector.close()` and `application_iter.close()`.

https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/blob/85dd69bda8f7591089ded638b67d57cf496676fb/src/werkzeug/serving.py#L343-L371

Catching `OSError` around that read and breaking out of the loop fixes it. I have that change with a test, and can open a PR against `stable` if that works for you.

Environment:

- Python version: 3.12.10 (macOS arm64)
- Werkzeug version: 3.1.9 (same code on `main`)

They currently store strings, then call `iri_to_uri` in `get_wsgi_headers`. And that's only done for WSGI, so sans-IO/ASGI doesn't get it. Instead, they should always be stored as URIs, and accessed as IRIs.

No other headers are "fixed" in `get_wsgi_headers`. `Response.headers` is considered "raw" values, where it's the responsibility of the code setting it to set a valid value. That's what the properties provide: set a Python value, get the right encoded header value.

`Response.response` has been annotated as `Iterable[bytes] | Iterable[str]` for a long time now. However, for historic reasons (Python 2's mixed str/bytes type, presumably), it can actually be a mixed `Iterable[bytes | str]`, because `Response.iter_encoded` does an instance check for every yielded item. While passing an iterable of strings is useful (for example, a generator with `csv.writer`), there should be absolutely no reason to have strings and bytes in the iterator. We could make `Response.iter_encoded` _hugely_ more efficient by only checking the type of the first item, then assuming it for the rest.

`direct_passthrough` is currently documented as useful for files, or for if you know the response is all bytes. With this change, it should only really be necessary for files/`wsgi.file_wrapper`. An iterator that just yields from another iterator (in the case of bytes) should be essentially no overhead.

comments.author: davidism
comments.body:
There's a ton of complexity around the response iterable that needs to be cleaned up and better documented.

- `is_sequence` (and `make_sequence`) only recognize `list` or `tuple`. This affects `automatically_set_content_length`, which could skip plenty of valid iterables that have a known length.
- `is_streamed` checks for `len` instead of `not Sequence`
- `calculate_content_length` isn't used anywhere, the code to calculate it is repeated in a few places.
- `make_sequence` defers the call to the original `response.close`. It should be closed immediately after iteration, the response already "owns" it and there's no reason to keep it open after the data has already been buffered. Other code that deals with iterables closes them immediately after iteration.
- The `automatically_set_content_length` flag shouldn't be needed. For example, `freeze` sets `content_length` regardless of if it's already set, which is correct because it just buffered and knows the exact length, regardless of what an existing header says. Meanwhile, other places can be switched by `automatically_set_content_length`, even though they would have the same guarantee at that point.
- 😵‍💫 `implicit_sequence_conversion`, `direct_passthrough`, `automatically_set_content_length`, `calculate_content_length`, `response`, `data`, `make_sequence`, `_ensure_sequence`, `iter_encoded`, `is_streamed`, `is_sequence`, `freeze`, `get_response_headers`, `get_app_iter` 😵‍💫 So many methods touch the response iterable in some way, documented at varying quality and detail, and I was only vaguely aware of most of them or how they interacted until I started looking at all of it in detail.

issue_body:
This tries to look like a writable binary file. It does not inherit from an `io` base class. Every call to `write` incurs a call to `_ensure_sequence` (and `is_sequence` and `isinstance`). It's not mentioned in documentation (beyond the autodoc) or examples. It has no equivalent in Quart.

It's entirely synchronous, all data would need to be written before returning the response. At that point there's no benefit to calling `write` repeatedly vs `set_data([list comprehension])`. Or use a generator, which can stream data as it's generated rather than needing to write it all up front.

It's very easy to end up producing a mixed str/bytes response, something that #3323 will deprecate. For example, if you start with `Response("Hello")`, that will be encoded early since it's a simple string, so `write(b"World")` is correct. But if you do `Response(["Hello", "World"])`, that will not be encoded since it's a sequence, so `response.write(b"Again")` will end up producing `[str, str, bytes]`.

Any library that provides a file-writing interface also provides a corresponding string/bytes function. Or you can write to `BytesIO` and return that with `send_file`.

It handles both evaluating preconditions and applying ranges. It does not match the order and logic in RFC9110 section 13 and 14. It looks like some of this confusion was due to trying to add range handling in to the existing conditional handling method, making the API a lot more complicated.

Some of the problems, and problems revealed in other parts of the code:

- Only applies to `GET` and `HEAD`, but conditional responses should apply to mutating methods as well.
- Processes range requests first, then conditional requests. This is backwards.
- Does not ensure the ETag being compared is strong/weak depending on what's being checked.
- `is_resource_modified` returns a bool, which is insufficient for the checks described in the spec. It needs to distinguish between 200, 304, 412, and 416. `make_conditional` tries to guess what status code to apply based on what `is_resource_modified` returns and what headers are set.
- Does not validate directly that the requested range unit is `bytes`. Allows setting `Accept-Ranges` to something besides `bytes` even though it will only handle bytes.
- Precedence of `If-Match` `If-Modified-Since` `If-Not-Match`, and `If-Unmodified-Since` is messed up.
- `is_resource_modified` doesn't take `if_unmodified_since`, so that header is completely ignored.
- `If-Range` date uses `<=` comparison instead of `==`.
- Sets the `Date` header for some reason. The spec does not mention this. Comments that servers will overwrite this, but doesn't explain why that's wrong. The date set by the server will not be meaningfully different from the date set here. `to_wsgi_response` doesn't set it, so it's not otherwise in-scope within Werkzeug.
- Similarly, sets `Content-Length`, but `to_wsgi_headers` already does that. But then again, `to_wsgi_headers` doesn't use `calculate_content_length`.
- Doesn't raise on 412, only sets the status code. So 412 still contains the original response's body and headers. `to_wsgi_response` doesn't handle clearing this like it does for 304.
- Invalid ranges produced 416, but that's only for valid but unsatisfiable ranges. Should return 200 for those.
- Considered multiple ranges invalid (and incorrectly returned 416). Spec says can either choose to ignore and return 200, or use first range only.
- Suffix range larger than the complete length was considered invalid instead of clamped.
- `ETagSet.contains/_weak` assume the given value had the correct weak/strong marker. Now that `ETag` exists, that can be passed and checked directly.
- `SharedDataMiddleware` tries to handle this again on its own, but only 304, doesn't support 412, 416, or ranges at all. Can use `send_file` instead.
- If `SharedDataMiddleware` wants to use `send_file`, `send_file` needs to be updated to handle file objects better. It can figure out their length, and potentially other properties through `os` functions on its handle.

This can be split into two new methods on `Response`, `apply_conditions(request)` and `apply_range(request)`. `make_conditional`, related helper methods, and `is_resource_modified`, can be deprecated.

comments.author: davidism
comments.body: After 412 handling was initially added, #1231 and https://github.com/pallets/flask/issues/2576 reported that 412 responses didn't have a body. The "fix" for that stopped removing the body for 412 in `get_app_iter`. However, `make_conditional` didn't clear the original body. What should have happened is it should have raised instead of setting the status on the existing request. That will be fixed now, so 412 will have a body (the error message) but a failed condition will not send the original body.

issue_body: While looking at #3284, I noticed this. This is incorrect, `SERVER_NAME` and `SERVER_PORT` refer to the local WSGI server. They're used as a fallback if the `Host` header isn't set, but that definitely will be set due to the `X-Forwarded-Host` header.

issue_title: `Request.application` doesn't type check when decorating a method
issue_body: `Request.application` supports decorating a function or a method. However, it's type annotation only accounts for a function. Needs to have overloads to support both.
It's a less powerful version of `Request.application`.

The `Request` `populate_request` argument adds `environ["werkzeug.request"] = self` on init. This isn't used anywhere.

- It's documented as being potentially useful for debugging, with no explanation how. With #3281, the goal is to pass around the request instead of the environ, then this won't be needed at all.
- It creates a reference loop, `environ` holds a reference to `request`, which holds a reference in `request.environ`. This is handled by the garbage collector, but it's not great.
- It's not guaranteed that `environ is environ["werkzeug.request"].environ`. For example, the test client copies the environ to isolate any changes the app makes, but doesn't update the cached request. Any middleware that didn't know about Werkzeug could result in the same thing.
- Any middleware that modifies the environ can result in the request having stale data either through init or cached properties.

I can't think of an easy way to deprecate the `werkzeug.request` key. Given that it's essentially undocumented and not used anywhere, I'm guessing that just removing it in 4.0 will be fine.

comments.author: davidism
comments.body:
`DebuggedApplication` actually has a `request_key="werkzeug.request"` parameter. It's documented as unused. I never encountered that while working on the debugger, so it's been more than a decade since it was used.

The i18nurls example project does use the key to automatically inject the request into a template render inside a custom `Response.__call__`. That does point out that it's safe to use the key if you know for sure there was nothing between the request creation and its use that would have any of the consequences listed above. However, with the way it's used there's no reason it couldn't have been passed as `req=request` in the constructor instead. Or injected by its dispatch as `app.template_ctx`, vaguely similar to how Flask works.

issue_body:
`contains` and `contains_weak` are the only correct methods, and match the strong and weak comparisons described in RFC 9110. None of the other methods are used by the code or required by any spec.

- `is_weak` is incorrect, it only checks if the value is in the weak set, but that's not the weak comparison function.
- `is_strong` is incorrect, it only checks if the value is in the strong set, but skips the star check.
- `contains_raw` decides what `contains` method to use based on if the parsed ETag is marked weak. But that's incorrect, which comparison to use is based on the header being evaluated, not the incoming ETag.
- `__call__` kind of fixes the problem with `contains_raw` by allowing to choose which comparison method to use with a parameter. But it also allows passing `data` to call `generate_etag`, which is not used anywhere and can be done as `contains(generate_etag(data))`.
- `as_set` loses weakness markers, meaning even if `include_weak=True` is passed it's impossible to tell what the data actually means unless you call it twice and subtract the sets.
- `__len__`, `__iter__`, and `__contains__` all act on the strong set only. But `__bool__` looks at the star tag and weak set too, which is correct for how this class is actually used. `__len__` and `__iter__` are incorrect, they don't represent how many values are contained in the collection (and can't with star), it's not clear why they would be used. `__contains__` is a less clear version of calling `contains`.
- `contains` should probably be renamed to `contains_strong` to mirror `contains_weak` and make it even clearer what's being used.
- With all that, there's no reason for this to inherit `Collection` at all.

It currently checks `text/html or accept_xhtml`. But HTML is not valid XHTML (or XML in general), so responding true if `application/xml` is asked for is wrong. It should only check `text/html`.

`accept_xhtml` should also be deprecated, XHTML is not something anyone's seeking out to use nowadays https://w3techs.com/technologies/details/ml-xhtml_any. I would be extremely surprised if any client was _requesting_ XHTML in `Accept`, or at least requesting it without also requesting HTML. Additionally, XHTML as used in practice is valid HTML, and it's unlikely an app would have a way to produce XHTML _or_ HTML based on the `Accept` header. And if they really need it, the app can still use `application/xhtml+xml in accept`.

While deprecating `environ_property`, I also [searched sourcegraph for uses of `header_property`](https://sourcegraph.com/search?q=context%3Aglobal+lang%3APython+%22werkzeug%22+%22header_property%22+-file%3Asite-packages%2F+-file%3Awerkzeug%2F+-file%3Aflask%2F+-repo%3A%5Egithub%5C.com%2Fpallets%2Fwerkzeug%24+&patternType=keyword&sm=0&__cc=1) and found zero. It's only very lightly documented, as in it's mentioned in the docs but has no explanation of how to use it. Presumably, people who want to work with other headers just work with them directly and don't make a whole `Request` subclass with a new property, or they do that but write the property directly for what they need.

We still use `header_property`, but that's because we're defining a _ton_ of properties at once in the same way. We can make it private instead of public.

This doesn't appear to be used, complicates the interface, and complicates type checking. `make_form_data_parser` expects to return a `FormDataParser` class, limiting how customization can be done (if it was done at all). `FormDataParser` isn't particularly designed for subclassing. It all ends up being used by the internal `_load_form_data`, which handles caching, empty data, or creates the class and calls its `parse` method. Instead, we can have it call a `_parse_form_data` method that returns the parsed form data or None. This can also remove the `want_form_data_parsed` property, which appears to be a holdover from a "stream only" mixin that was removed ages ago.

- No uses of setting `form_data_parser_class` https://sourcegraph.com/search?q=context:global+lang:Python+%22form_data_parser_class%22+-file:site-packages/+-file:werkzeug/+-file:flask/+-repo:^github\.com/pallets/werkzeug%24+&patternType=keyword&sm=0
- No uses of overriding `make_form_data_parser` https://sourcegraph.com/search?q=context:global+lang:Python+%22make_form_data_parser%22+-file:site-packages/+-file:werkzeug/+-file:flask/+-repo:%5Egithub%5C.com/pallets/werkzeug%24+&patternType=keyword&sm=0
- No uses of overriding `want_form_data_parsed` https://sourcegraph.com/search?q=context:global+lang:Python+%22want_form_data_parsed%22+-file:site-packages/+-file:werkzeug/+-file:flask/+-repo:%5Egithub%5C.com/pallets/werkzeug%24+&patternType=keyword&sm=0

comments.body: @pgjones I don't think this will affect Quart, beyond needing `async def _parse_form_data` instead.

comments.author: davidism
comments.body:
`default_stream_factory` doesn't use `max_form_memory_size`, so everyone was always getting 500 kB in-memory files regardless of the setting (although parsing would have stopped at that point). Of course stream factory takes four arguments that no one probably uses, and doesn't take that one. Customizing `stream_factory` does appear to happen a few times (still extremely uncommon) so I don't want to deprecate it. But we should deprecate `default_stream_factory` in favor of `FormDataParser` building a function that uses `max_form_memory_size` if nothing was passed.

`max_form_memory_size` can be `None`, which suggests that the factory should return `BytesIO` in that case. I decided against that for now, it's probably better to keep the 500 kB default.

issue_body:
- `input_stream` is explicitly documented as unsafe compared to its wrapped counterpart in `stream`.
- `remote_user` is only mentioned in passing as part of CGI that WSGI accepts for compatibility.
- `is_multithread`, `is_multiprocess`, and `is_run_once` are about how the server is running workers. But I can't think of how that matters to the application, code must avoid globals and use external storage regardless of the worker type.
- All of these can be accessed directly from `request.environ` if needed, they even still have their correct types.
- I can't find any uses of `environ_property` (or `header_property`) in external code.
- None of the many other WSGI and CGI keys are exposed.
- ASGI has no concept of any of these.

User agent parsing was removed in 2.0 in 2021 in #2078. The intention was that `Request.user_agent_class` could be set to a subclass of `UserAgent` that parsed and populated the other properties. The full string could be accessed with `request.user_agent.string`.

This never seems to have been adopted. There are no meaningful results in https://sourcegraph.com/search?q=context:global+lang:Python+%22user_agent_class%22+-file:site-packages/+-file:werkzeug/+-file:flask/+-repo:%5Egithub%5C.com/pallets/werkzeug%24+&patternType=keyword&sm=0 (and half of those are unrelated to Werkzeug). Searching for "werkzeug user agent" or "werkzeug user_agent_class" on search engines or PyPI brings up nothing.

This isn't particularly good for type checking, as `Request` would need to be generic on `user_agent_class` in order for a subclass to expose more properties. It saves approximately one line over parsing the user agent string directly, and requires implementing an interface that might not fit what you need anyway.

Deprecate this and make `Request.user_agent` a string. `UserAgent` can subclass `str` during the deprecation, and warn when accessing `user_agent.string`.

This was disabled by default in 2.1 in 2022. There doesn't seem to be any reason to produce absolute redirect URLs now. The only issue reported, in 2023, was it had previously obscured an open redirect bug in another library, and that should have been addressed at the browser level as well.

Code search shows exactly three uses of setting it to `True` https://sourcegraph.com/search?q=context:global+lang:Python+%22autocorrect_location_header+%3D+True%22+-file:site-packages/+-file:werkzeug/+-file:flask/+-repo:%5Egithub%5C.com/pallets/werkzeug%24+&patternType=keyword&sm=0 Two of them have no apparent use, the third is a temporary workaround related to the issue mentioned above. Searching for only `autocorrect_location_header` shows that every other use is setting it to `False`. If it's truly needed, `response.location = url_for(..., _external=True)` or `urljoin(request.host, response.location)` will do it explicitly.

A side note, `Response.autocorrect_location_header` doesn't know about `trusted_hosts`, so it will use whatever `Host` is sent. This doesn't actually mean anything in practice, since it only affects the requests you make, and your browser or code would be sending a trusted `Host` header.

This is a more conservative version of #3237 that only fixes bugs/unintended behavior and otherwise doesn't break existing URLs. I'll target this at 3.2 since it does change what's accept a bit still.

- Non-ASCII digits are accepted.
- `int(fixed_digits=4, signed=True)` counts the negative sign as a digit.
- `float` overflow values (too large to fit in float) become `inf`, which is a special, unexpected value that can cause problems when used later on.
  - Underflow values become `0.0`, which is a "normal" value.
  - Binary float cannot represent all values, but that's a very abstract concept for users to understand and ensure in URLs.
- #3147 prevented scientific notation by limiting to 6 decimal places, which excludes many legitimate values.

A 1-to-1 mapping of URLs to parsed values is not a goal. This will be documented for these converters. However, `.4` and `4.` will remain disallowed, I want to keep the more obvious `left.right` syntax only. And `4.` would cause issues with Markdown URL detection.

The private `NumberConverter` base seems to be more trouble than the small amount of duplication it removes, especially if we also tried to extend it to `decimal` later, so I'll remove it.

comments.body:
I couldn't reproduce this at first, I realized that somehow your Python build doesn't include `cProfile`, so it falls back to `profile`. And only `profile` raises the warning.

It looks like you're also not building `profiling.tracing`? You should probably fix that, as there won't be a fallback module anymore. If you fix that, it will also solve this, as `cProfile` remains available on all versions (`profiling.tracing` is a rename of it).
